prompt: About what percentage of men of Northern European descent have red-green colour vision deficiency?
Why is red-green deficiency much more common in men than in women?

choices.why: It is inherited, not acquired.

choices.text: It is inherited on the X chromosome
choices.why: Right. Men have one X, so one affected copy is enough.
The number of cones is not the reason.

choices.text: It is caused by age, and men live less
choices.why: It is present from birth.

prompt: In the simulated chart, what still differed between the two olive lines?

choices.why: Right, which is why palettes should differ in lightness, not only in hue.

Both were solid lines.

prompt: Which form of colour vision deficiency is the most common?

choices.why: Blue-yellow deficiency is rare.
Seeing no colour at all is very rare.
Protan forms exist but are less common than deutan ones.
Right, a shifted medium-wavelength cone.

prompt: What contrast ratio does WCAG 2.2 level AA ask for ordinary text, as the first number of the ratio?
What contrast does WCAG 2.2 ask for a bar or line that the reader needs?

choices.why: That is for text.
21:1 is black on white, the maximum.
Right, criterion 1.4.11, Non-text Contrast.
Graphics a reader needs are covered.

prompt: Red and blue have a contrast of 1.04:1, yet they still separate two series for deuteranopia. Why?

choices.text: Their contrast rises to 4.5:1 when simulated
choices.why: It rises only to 1.24:1.
Right: olive and blue. Contrast measures only lightness.
Blue is seen; the blue cones are unaffected.

choices.text: Contrast below 3:1 does not matter for lines
choices.why: It matters against the background; between two lines, hue can also separate them.

prompt: Lesson 13's context grey, #c8ccd4, measured 1.61:1 on white. What does the lesson conclude?

choices.text: It passes, because context bars are decoration
choices.why: The context is what gives the highlight its meaning, so it is needed.
Every pair is above 1; the threshold is 3.
Right. Chosen by eye, it is too quiet for a mark the reader needs, and the context is lost.

choices.text: It fails only for colour-blind readers
choices.why: It fails for everybody's eyes: 1.61 as most people see it.

prompt: What does WCAG criterion 1.4.1, Use of Color, require?

choices.text: Charts use at most two colours
choices.why: It sets no limit on the number of colours.
They are allowed with a second cue.

choices.text: Every chart has a grey version
choices.why: A grey version is a useful check, not the requirement.

choices.text: Colour is never the only carrier of meaning
choices.why: Right. Colour plus something.

prompt: Which second cue removes the colour lookup altogether?

choices.why: A legend is still matched by colour.
Brighter red and green are still confused.

choices.text: A direct label on each line
choices.why: Right. The line says what it is.

choices.text: A thicker line for each series
choices.why: Equal thickness on both does not separate them.

prompt: A status column shows on-target items in green and late items in red. What fixes it best?

choices.why: Colour is still the only carrier.

choices.text: Add a word or a symbol
choices.why: Right: "late", or a down arrow. The meaning survives when the colour does not.
Colour helps most readers; the rule asks for colour plus something.

choices.text: Explain the colours in a footnote
choices.why: A reader who cannot tell them apart still cannot use the explanation.

prompt: Which text alternative is best for a bar chart of growth by region?

choices.text: One naming the chart, its finding and key values
choices.why: Right. What it is, what it shows, the numbers to quote.
True and useless.
It says what the chart is, not what it shows.

choices.text: The file name of the image
choices.why: A file name tells a screen-reader user nothing.

prompt: A heatmap has 105 cells. What should accompany its short text alternative?

choices.text: A longer alternative listing all 105 values
choices.why: Too long to listen to; a table is navigable.

choices.text: Nothing more; heatmaps are visual by nature
choices.why: Readers who cannot see it still need its data.
Right, and the alternative keeps to the finding.
A grey picture does not help a screen reader.

prompt: What can axe not measure on this platform's pages?

choices.text: The contrast of a button label
choices.why: That is exactly what axe measures.
axe finds those.

choices.text: Text drawn inside an SVG figure
choices.why: Right, which is why the figures have their own contrast check.

choices.text: A heading that skips a level
choices.why: axe finds those too.

prompt: A locked course card was faded to show it was locked. What did the check find, and what replaced the fade?

choices.text: Low contrast; a word and a border
choices.why: Right: 4.09:1 dark and 3.32:1 light.

choices.text: Nothing was wrong; the fade stayed
choices.why: The fade took the text below 4.5:1 in both themes.

choices.text: The card was hidden from students
choices.why: It stays visible, with its state in words.
Any fade lowers contrast; the fix was to stop fading.
